problemStatement.formal: f(k) = (1 + o(1)) · e/(e-1) · k where f(k) = min largest denominator in 1 = Σ 1/nᵢ
problemStatement.plain: Let f(k) be the minimal value of the largest denominator among all representations 1 = 1/n₁ + ··· + 1/nₖ. Is f(k) = (1+o(1)) · e/(e-1) · k? YES (Martin 2000).
whyMatters: Egyptian fractions are a classical topic connecting number theory and combinatorics
The constant e/(e-1) arises from the harmonic series structure
Martin's 2000 proof resolves a question Erdős asked about optimal representations

proven: Egyptian constant algebraic identities (eq, inv, one_plus_inv)
Valid lengths k=0,2,3,4,5 with explicit witnesses
k=1 is NOT valid (proved by contradiction)
Main asymptotic from axiom: f(k) = (1+o(1)) · e/(e-1) · k
open: Martin's theorem itself (axiomatized, deep number-theoretic result)

insights: e/(e-1) arises because ln(e·u) - ln(e) = 1, making [e, e·u] contain ~1 unit of harmonic mass
Real.exp_one_gt_d9 and exp_one_lt_d9 give tight bounds on e for nlinarith proofs
k=1 impossibility: 1/a + 1/b = 1 with a<b has unique solution a=b=2, contradicting a<b
Egyptian fraction splitting: 1/n = 1/(n+1) + 1/(n(n+1)) enables generating larger k witnesses
